The Sarcolab pilot study of 2 crewmembers, investigated before and after a 6-mo International Space Station mission, has demonstrated the substantial muscle wasting and weakness, along with disruption of muscle’s oxidative metabolism. The present work aimed at evaluating the pro/anti-inflammatory status in the same 2 crewmembers (A, B). Blood circulating (c-)microRNAs (miRs), c-proteasome, c-mitochondrial DNA, and cytokines were assessed by real-time quantitative PCR or ELISA tests. Time series analysis was performed ( i.e. , before flight and after landing) at 1 and 15 d of recovery (R+1 and R+15, respectively). C-biomarkers were compared with an age-matched control population and with 2-dimensional proteomic analysis of the 2 crewmembers’ muscle biopsies. Striking differences were observed between the 2 crewmembers at R+1, in terms of inflamma-miRs (c-miRs-21-5p, -126-3p, and -146a-5p), muscle specific (myo)-miR-206, c-proteasome, and IL-6/leptin, thus making the 2 astronauts dissimilar to each other. Final recovery levels of c-proteasome, c-inflamma-miRs, and c-myo-miR-206 were not reverted to the baseline values in crewmember A. In both crewmembers, myo-miR-206 changed significantly after recovery. Muscle biopsy of astronaut A showed an impressive 80% increase of α-1-antitrypsin, a target of miR-126-3p. These results point to a strong stress response induced by spaceflight involving muscle tissue and the proinflammatory setting, where inflamma-miRs and myo-miR-206 mediate the systemic recovery phase after landing.—Capri, M., Morsiani, C., Santoro, A., Moriggi, M., Conte, M., Martucci, M., Bellavista, E., Fabbri, C., Giampieri, E., Albracht, K., Flück, M., Ruoss, S., Brocca, L., Canepari, M., Longa, E., Di Giulio, I., Bottinelli, R., Cerretelli, P., Salvioli, S., Gelfi, C., Franceschi, C., Narici, M., Rittweger, J. Recovery from 6-month spaceflight at the International Space Station: muscle-related stress into a proinflammatory setting. microRNA-206 • inflamma-miRs • proteasome • SERPINA1 SJS Export v1 It is known that short- and long-term spaceflights are associated with physiologic and biologic changes of the human body ( 1 – 3 ). Currently, long-term orbiting flights are regularly performed to serve the International Space Station (ISS) missions, and deep space missions ( e.g. , to the moon or Mars) are thought to be feasible soon ( 4 ). Among the many bodily effects, those related to the skeletal-muscle apparatus and brain appear to be particularly relevant in terms of possible health risks and difficulty to revert the changes after landing ( 5 ). Many of the space-related changes are detrimental to the body, and it has been suggested that microgravity could be seen as a model of ageing ( 6 ). Access to astronauts is quite limited, which is a considerable impediment to the generation of knowledge in space medicine. Luckily, the possibility of measuring advanced blood biomarkers, such as microRNAs (miRs), and pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines offer the intriguing opportunity of easily monitoring crew health concerning the physiologic and stress-associated challenges of spaceflight. In addition, circulating (c-)markers are promising tools for the evaluation of healthy and unhealthy ageing trajectories ( 7 ). Thus, blood is an informative tissue in which the presence and the concentration of markers may indicate not only tissue/organ injuries or suffering status but also epigenetic changes that may propagate in all the body, especially in the case of c-miRs. In fact, many of these molecules are able to modulate inflammatory signaling pathways, in particular the inflamma-miRs (miR-21-5p, -126-3p, -146a-5p), which were found to be increased or dysregulated in the blood with ageing or pathologic conditions ( 8 ). The Sarcolab pilot study has studied the neuromuscular adaptations to long-term space flight in 2 crewmembers before and after a 6-mo ISS mission and has demonstrated substantial muscle wasting and weakness, along with disruption of muscle’s oxidative metabolism, as a result of spaceflight ( 9 ). The muscle atrophy observed with spaceflight has some analogy with the age-associated loss of muscle mass (sarcopenia) ( 10 ). In both conditions, the loss of muscle mass could contribute to the increase of c-markers networking with the stress response and proinflammatory status as well as inflammageing along with life span ( 11 – 13 ). Further support for such a view is provided by the recent observation that body core temperature is increased in space in a way that is independent of impeded heat dissipation and which seems to be linked with an inflammatory response ( 14 ). The driving hypothesis is that spaceflight, as a prolonged stressor, and recovery may favor a proinflammatory status, increasing the molecular “garbage,” such as misplaced molecules ( 15 ), which in turn may favor the inflammatory stress conditions. To this purpose, the present work attempts to evaluate the pro- and anti-inflammatory status in the 2 crewmembers (A and B) who spent ∼6 mo in space. Blood c-miRs, c-proteasome, c-mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), and cytokines were evaluated before flight and after 1 and 15 d of recovery and correlated with muscle proteomic analysis. All data were acquired taking into account the main question: How similar are the 2 crewmembers’ responses to spaceflight and recovery after 1 and 15 d from landing?

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the pro/anti-inflammatory status and molecular changes, including circulating microRNAs (miRs), proteasome, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), cytokines, and muscle proteomic changes, in two crewmembers after a 6-month International Space Station mission. The aim was to evaluate systemic and muscle-related stress responses and recovery patterns, comparing biomarkers at 1 day (R+1) and 15 days (R+15) post-landing with pre-flight values and age-matched controls. Findings revealed a strong spaceflight-induced stress response in muscle tissue, leading to a proinflammatory state, with inflamma-miRs and myo-miR-206 mediating systemic recovery, and significant inter-individual differences in biomarker responses were observed.

treatment_details.therapy_type: 6-month International Space Station (ISS) spaceflight exposure with in-flight countermeasure training, followed by a post-flight recovery period.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Two crewmembers were exposed to approximately 6 months of spaceflight. Samples were collected pre-flight (76-79 days before) and post-flight at 1 day (R+1 / 24 hours) and 15 days (R+15) after landing. Individual molecular responses varied significantly between the two crewmembers, with crewmember A generally showing more persistent changes. Specifics of in-flight countermeasure training dose were not detailed, and no dose-response comparisons for spaceflight duration were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher, with striking differences between crewmembers. Significantly increased in crewmember A at R+1 and showed highest levels at R+15, failing to revert to baseline. Changes in crewmember B were not significant, suggesting individual differences.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Modulates inflammatory signaling pathways and immune response, identified as an inflamma-miR. Involved in cell proliferation, osteogenic differentiation, and part of the 'response to stress' gene ontology, targeting CLOCK (circadian rhythm regulator).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-spaceflight recovery (R+1 and R+15) in crewmembers A and B, associated with a proinflammatory setting and tissue/cell injury.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Mediates systemic recovery post-spaceflight, indicating a delayed or persistent inflammatory and stress response in crewmember A, reflecting an unbalancing of homeostasis and contributing to inter-individual dissimilarity. It is also linked to osteogenic differentiation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher, with significant increases observed at R+1 in both crewmembers. While crewmember B showed complete recovery, levels in crewmember A were not reverted to baseline at R+15, with highest levels observed at this time point.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Modulates inflammatory signaling pathways and is crucial for vascular integrity and angiogenesis. Classified as an inflamma-miR and part of the 'response to stress' gene ontology, it targets "alpha-1-antitrypsin" (SERPINA1).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-spaceflight recovery (R+1 and R+15) in crewmembers A and B, associated with a proinflammatory setting.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Mediates systemic recovery and indicates a sustained inflammatory/stress response and impaired recovery in crewmember A compared to B, highlighting differential physiological adaptation and an unbalancing of homeostasis. It is also potentially involved in tissue-related anti-inflammatory response regulation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher, with significant increases at R+1 in both crewmembers. Crewmember B showed complete recovery, but levels in crewmember A were not reverted to baseline at R+15, showing highest levels at this time point.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Modulates inflammatory signaling pathways and acts as a key negative regulator of innate immune responses. Classified as an inflamma-miR and part of the 'response to stress' gene ontology, it is involved in systemic recovery and inflammation, targeting CLOCK.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-spaceflight recovery (R+1 and R+15) in crewmembers A and B, associated with a proinflammatory setting and tissue/cell injury.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Mediates systemic recovery, indicating a persistent inflammatory/stress response in crewmember A compared to B, signifying differential physiological stress coping mechanisms and an unbalancing of homeostasis.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher and changed significantly after recovery in both crewmembers, with striking differences observed at R+1. Significantly increased in crewmember A at both R+1 and R+15, and still increased at R+15 in both, but not reverted to baseline in crewmember A.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A muscle-specific microRNA, preferentially expressed in skeletal muscle. It mediates systemic recovery, promotes cell differentiation, inhibits cell growth, and is involved in muscle development, regeneration, and response to injury, increasing in catabolic/atrophy conditions.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-spaceflight recovery (R+1 and R+15) in crewmembers A and B, associated with muscle-related stress, muscle atrophy, and physical training status.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Mediates the systemic recovery phase after landing, indicating muscle atrophy/wasting and muscle-related stress response. It highlights significant and sustained molecular changes in crewmember A compared to B, suggesting differences in muscle adaptation, recovery, and suitability for monitoring skeletal muscle status.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher, with significant increases in both crewmembers at R+1. Crewmember B recovered, but crewmember A showed further, sustained increases at R+15, failing to revert to baseline and reaching concentrations similar to those seen in autoimmune disease.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Involved in protein degradation pathways and stress response, often indicating cellular stress or damage. It also mediates inflammatory pathways, representing a general mechanism to initiate inflammation and immune cell activities.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-spaceflight recovery (R+1 and R+15) in crewmembers A and B, associated with a strong stress response and potential muscle wasting during a 6-month ISS mission.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a strong stress response induced by spaceflight, persistent cellular stress, and protein turnover issues in crewmember A, highlighting differential recovery and contributing to inter-individual dissimilarity. It serves as a marker of muscle wasting, potential muscle recovery, systemic stress/inflammation, and unbalancing of homeostasis.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher and dysregulated, with striking differences between crewmembers. Significantly increased at R+1 in crewmember A, then recovered, but showed no change in crewmember B.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A proinflammatory cytokine that plays a crucial role in immune responses, acute phase reactions, metabolism, and bone turnover.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates an acute inflammatory response in crewmember A that recovered, while crewmember B showed no significant change, highlighting differing immune system responses to spaceflight. It is involved in the proinflammatory status induced by spaceflight, systemic stress/inflammation, and bone turnover, and suggests an unbalancing of homeostasis.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher and dysregulated, with striking differences between crewmembers. Significantly increased at R+1 in crewmember A, then recovered, but showed no change in crewmember B.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Primarily produced by adipose cells, it regulates energy balance, appetite, metabolism, and is involved in inflammation and bone turnover. It is also part of the stress response and homeostasis regulation.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests an acute metabolic or physiological stress response in crewmember A that recovered, while crewmember B remained stable, indicating individual differences in metabolic adaptation to spaceflight. It is involved in systemic changes during spaceflight recovery, inflammation, bone turnover, systemic stress/inflammation, and unbalancing of homeostasis.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher, with an impressive 80% increase in astronaut A's muscle biopsy. More abundant in crewmember A after landing (+66% at R+1, +81% at R+15) and increased in crewmember B only at final recovery (+23% at R+15).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A serine protease inhibitor and acute phase protein, involved in anti-inflammatory response and acting as a stress and antioxidant protein. It is a validated target of miR-126-3p.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a strong stress response and tissue-related anti-inflammatory response in muscle tissue following spaceflight, linked to inflammatory regulation via miR-126-3p, and shows differences in stress and antioxidant proteins post-spaceflight.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: While not significantly modified in either crewmember compared to controls, values for crewmember A were dramatically evident and at the extreme limit of the normal range, indicating a subtle increase.
